extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of public relations (newswriting for broadcast)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating Video News Releases (VNRs) intended for television newsrooms, covering strategic aims, structural elements, production choices, and broadcast scriptwriting rules. Useful for PR students, agency producers, and communications professionals producing broadcast-ready video press materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid being too promotional
rubrics_metrics.description: So. How do you get all or part of a VNR on the air? Simply put, avoid being too promotional. If it is, it will be viewed as an advertisement rather than “news”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: overt marketing copy or sales pitches that make the piece look like an ad. Scoring note: the more the VNR reads/looks like independent news rather than a commercial, the more likely a newsroom will use it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include a professional news reporter (or an actor) on camera
rubrics_metrics.description: It should include a professional news reporter who has on-air experience with news or an actor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: makes the VNR look like a real news report. Example: use a credible on-air presence rather than an obviously promotional spokesperson.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use expert interviews with legitimate expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: It might have an interview with an expert on the topic who has legitimate expertise in the subject, although he might be somewhat biased.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: choose experts with real credentials and clear relevance; disclose potential bias contextually. Newsrooms value perceived authority even if partial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate products or services when relevant
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrations of the products or services that are the subject of the VNR.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tip: show the product in use so journalists and viewers see what you want emphasized; keep demonstrations realistic and newsy rather than purely promotional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid overproducing the video
rubrics_metrics.description: In addition to not making it too promotional, you also want to avoid overproducing. Remember, news footage is usually fairly “raw” and an overly produced video will prevent the local news team from putting their own spin on it, which is what they want to do.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: slick, highly produced pieces that leave no room for newsroom editing. Keep footage naturalistic and editable so stations can integrate or repackage it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat VNR script like any television script (write for eye and ear)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writing a video news release script is exactly the same as writing a television script for any purpose. The first and most important thing to remember is that you are writing for the eye and ear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: craft visuals and audio together; ensure images match spoken copy; consider pacing and timing for broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use conversational writing (write the way you talk)
rubrics_metrics.description: The writing style should be conversational. Write the way you talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid formal, dense or literary prose; prefer spoken-language rhythms and contractions where appropriate to sound natural on air.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep sentences brief (20 words or less) and one idea per sentence
rubrics_metrics.description: Each sentence should be brief – 20 words or less -- and contain only one idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring note: tight sentences increase clarity for listeners and reduce risk of pronunciation/reading errors on camera. Edit for single-idea sentences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be simple and direct
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid jargon, long clauses, and convoluted phrasing; prioritize clearness over flourish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be brief — accomodate broadcast time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Be brief. The story that may get hundreds – even thousands – of words in a newspaper may have only 30 seconds – or less
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical exercise: write to a target running time (e.g., 30 seconds); cut nonessential detail; prioritize core facts and visuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put important information first (use inverted pyramid)
rubrics_metrics.description: Put the important information first. The inverted pyramid style is crucial for broadcast news.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lead with the most newsworthy elements so editors can truncate the tail; structure copy so content can be cut from the end if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a person’s complete name on first reference, then last name thereafter
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a person’s complete name on first reference, then their last name thereafter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style rule for clarity in spoken copy—avoid repeating full names after initial introduction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide phonetic spelling for unfamiliar or hard-to-pronounce words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use phonetic spelling for unfamiliar words and those that are hard to pronounce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical tip: include phonetics in the script handed to on-air talent to avoid mispronunciations during reads.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put titles before names
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles precede names: “Washington Mayor Joel Whitaker” not “Joel Whitaker, mayor of Washington.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: spoken copy flows better and immediate context is given; follow this ordering in scripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid direct quotations; prefer sound bites
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid direct quotations in a news script if possible. Instead, use a sound bite instead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance: use short, punchy recorded sound bites from sources rather than long quoted blocks; minimize scripted quotes to keep naturalness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid almost every abbreviation; write out dates/places/titles and hyphenate abbreviations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid almost every abbreviation. Write out day, months, states and military titles. Hyphenate abbreviations: “The student was a member of the P-G-C-C basketball team.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style guidance: in spoken copy, spelled-out forms/readable formats are clearer. When abbreviations are necessary, present them in a pronounceable, hyphenated or clarified form.
